summary: Describes an envelope that binds a file to one or more time-stamp tokens obtained for it, as defined in RFC 3161 or its successors. The file does not need to be cryptographically protected, and other kinds of temporal evidence are allowed too.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5544 defines a container that binds a document to evidence of when it existed. The container can include the document itself or a URI to it, plus time-stamp tokens and optional metadata.

subtitle: A CMS envelope that stores a document with its time-stamp evidence.

tldr.problem: A time-stamp can show that a file existed by a certain time, but keeping the file and its time-stamps together has often required separate files or application-specific formats.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5544 defines a CMS TimeStampedData object that can contain a file or its URI, optional metadata and one or more forms of temporal evidence.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational, was updated by RFC 5955 and is not a candidate for Internet Standard status. The IESG note points to RFC 4998 as an alternative.

today: RFC 5544 is Informational and was updated by RFC 5955. It is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard; the IESG note encourages readers to also review RFC 4998.

sections.title: Keeping a File with Its Time-Stamp
sections.content:
A time-stamp can provide evidence that a document existed before a particular time. It can apply to an unsigned document or to a complete signed document.

RFC 5544 addresses the difficulty of keeping time-stamps with a document. It defines a CMS-based envelope that binds a file to its temporal evidence instead of leaving users to manage separate files or application-specific containers.
sections.plainLanguage: The time-stamp and the file need to stay associated so the evidence can be checked against the right document. This RFC defines one format to keep them together.

sections.title: The TimeStampedData Object
sections.content:
The new CMS content type is called timestamped-data. Its TimeStampedData structure contains version, an optional dataUri, optional metadata, optional content and temporalEvidence. If content is absent, dataUri must identify where the document can be retrieved.

Metadata can include a file name, media type and other attributes. Temporal evidence can be an RFC 3161 time-stamp-token chain, an Evidence Record or another identified type. Compliant applications must support the RFC 3161 evidence form.
sections.plainLanguage: The container can carry the document or point to it, describe it and include evidence about its time. Applications are required to support the time-stamp-token form of evidence.

sections.title: How Time-Stamp Tokens Link Together
sections.content:
The first token covers the document contents. If metadata is present and hashProtected is true, the first token covers the DER-encoded metadata followed by the document contents.

Each later token covers the preceding TimeStampAndCRL element. An optional certificate revocation list can accompany a token to show the status of the time-stamping authority's certificate when the next element was added.
sections.plainLanguage: The first token is calculated from the document, and later tokens are calculated from the previous evidence entry. This creates a chain that can be checked in order.

sections.title: Creating, Checking and Extending Evidence
sections.content:
To create an object, an application selects whether to include the file or provide a dataUri, computes the required digest, obtains a time-stamp token from a time-stamping authority and places the result inside the CMS content type.

To verify it, an application checks the content type and version, retrieves the file if needed, recomputes the digest and validates each token and its signer. To extend the chain, it validates existing evidence and adds a new token over the most recent element.
sections.plainLanguage: To check the evidence, retrieve the file if needed and compare its digest with the first token. Then check each later token against the entry before it.

sections.title: What Time-Stamp Evidence Does Not Prove
sections.content:
If metadata is hash-protected, a later change can be detected. This does not prove that the metadata was correct when the object was created; that must be assessed from other information.

The RFC says a token should generally not be considered valid after its authority's certificate expires. A chain can extend the evidence, but each new token must be added before the previous one expires or is revoked, and suitable revocation information must be retained.
sections.plainLanguage: A protected digest can show that metadata has not changed, but it cannot show that the metadata was true at the start. Evidence chains also need new tokens and certificate-status information in time.
